content:
Quick answer: Many popular arthritis diet claims are not supported by evidence. Nightshade vegetables, citrus fruit and gluten have not been shown to worsen arthritis for most people; apple cider vinegar and manuka honey have no evidence of benefit; and no diet or supplement cures arthritis or replaces medicines. What does help is a balanced, Mediterranean-style diet, oily fish, and a healthy weight.

Evidence checked on 10 October 2026 against Arthritis UK's diet information, NICE NG100, NICE NG226 and NHS guidance.

When you live with arthritis, you will hear a lot of diet advice: from friends, social media, magazines and well-meaning relatives. Some of it is helpful. A lot of it is not, and some can lead people to cut out nutritious foods, spend money they do not need to, or feel that their pain is their own fault. This guide checks 16 popular claims against the evidence.

Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) sums it up: there are no diets or supplements that will cure arthritis, but some people find their condition is affected by what they eat, how much they weigh and how active they are.

Myth 1: "Tomatoes, potatoes and other nightshades make arthritis worse"

Verdict: not supported. Arthritis UK says research has shown no link between inflammation and nightshade (solanaceous) vegetables, which include tomatoes, potatoes, peppers and aubergines. They contain important vitamins and minerals. Food allergies linked to this family are possible, so if you notice a clear reaction, speak to a healthcare professional. Our guide to foods that may trigger symptoms explains how to test a suspected food safely rather than cutting out whole groups.

Myth 2: "Citrus fruit and acidic foods cause joint inflammation"

Verdict: not supported. Arthritis UK says there is no clear link between citrus fruit and inflammation, and some evidence that citrus may reduce the risk of inflammatory arthritis. Citrus fruits provide vitamin C, which helps absorb iron from plant foods. Allergy is possible but uncommon. Note that grapefruit can interact with some medicines, including ciclosporin, colchicine and warfarin, which is a medicine issue, not an inflammation one.

Myth 3: "Everyone with arthritis should go gluten-free"

Verdict: not supported for most people. Arthritis UK says there is no research directly linking gluten to any type of arthritis. However, coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition, and people with one autoimmune condition, including some types of inflammatory arthritis and Sjögren's, may be at slightly higher risk of another. If you have tummy pain, diarrhoea, bloating or unexplained weight loss, ask your GP to test for coeliac disease before you cut out gluten, because the test needs you to be eating gluten to be accurate.

Myth 4: "Dairy causes inflammation and should be avoided"

Verdict: mixed evidence; not a reason to cut it out. Arthritis UK says research on dairy-free diets is mixed. Dairy foods are a major source of calcium, and many people with arthritis are at higher risk of osteoporosis. If you feel unwell after dairy, you could be lactose intolerant. If you do avoid dairy, choose calcium-fortified alternatives and consider advice from a dietitian.

Myth 5: "Apple cider vinegar cures arthritis"

Verdict: no evidence. Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that apple cider vinegar improves arthritis symptoms, and it can be expensive. Drinking it undiluted can also irritate your throat and teeth.

Myth 6: "Manuka honey reduces joint inflammation"

Verdict: no evidence. Arthritis UK says the same about manuka honey. It is also a source of free sugars; the NHS says adults should have no more than 30g of free sugars a day.

Myth 7: "The right diet can replace arthritis medicines"

Verdict: false, and potentially harmful. NICE guidance on rheumatoid arthritis says there is no strong evidence that diet changes will benefit arthritis, and that complementary therapies should not replace conventional treatment. Arthritis UK says changing your diet probably will not have as great an impact as medical treatment and you should not stop any treatments. In inflammatory arthritis, untreated disease can cause permanent joint damage.

Myth 8: "There is one special arthritis diet that works for everyone"

Verdict: false. Arthritis UK points out that there are many types of arthritis and differences between people, so what works for one person may not work for another. The best-supported approach is a balanced, Mediterranean-style diet, which NICE suggests for people with rheumatoid arthritis who want to change their diet. See our anti-inflammatory diet guide.

Myth 9: "Cod liver oil is good for osteoarthritis"

Verdict: not supported. Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that cod liver oil makes a difference to osteoarthritis, and large doses of fish liver oil could lead to too much vitamin A, which is particularly risky in pregnancy. Pure fish oil (not liver oil) has some evidence in rheumatoid arthritis. See our omega-3 evidence review.

Myth 10: "Glucosamine and collagen rebuild cartilage"

Verdict: not supported. NICE guidance on osteoarthritis (NG226) says glucosamine should not be offered, because there is no strong evidence of benefit. Arthritis UK says there is currently no good evidence that collagen supplements can rebuild cartilage that has already been damaged, and that the NHS does not recommend collagen for arthritis. Some people report symptom benefits, but research is mixed.

Myth 11: "Food allergies cause rheumatoid arthritis"

Verdict: not supported. Arthritis UK says some people believe allergies or intolerances worsen conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, but there is no research to support this. People with arthritis can also have allergies or intolerances, which a doctor or dietitian can help identify. Elimination diets have sometimes helped people with rheumatoid arthritis, but the foods involved differ between people, and Arthritis UK says there is no evidence they help osteoarthritis.

Myth 12: "A detox, juice cleanse or alkaline diet will flush out inflammation"

Verdict: not supported. Your liver and kidneys remove waste products; there is no good evidence that detox products or "alkalising" foods change joint inflammation. Juices are high in free sugars, and the NHS suggests limiting fruit juice and smoothies to a combined total of 150ml a day. Very restrictive regimes can also cause unplanned weight loss.

Myth 13: "Probiotics and gut supplements fix arthritis"

Verdict: not proven. Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that changing the gut microbiome affects autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, and probiotics have not been shown to help. The NHS advises people with a weakened immune system, including those on some arthritis medicines, to talk to a doctor before taking probiotics. See our gut health guide.

Myth 14: "Weight does not matter if you have inflammatory arthritis"

Verdict: false. NICE says weight loss improves pain, function and quality of life for people with osteoarthritis who are living with overweight or obesity. Arthritis UK says excess weight can also increase inflammation and is linked to a higher risk of rheumatoid arthritis and gout. Being underweight is also a concern, as it is linked with fracture risk.

Myth 15: "You must cut out red meat completely if you have rheumatoid arthritis"

Verdict: not supported. Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that avoiding foods such as red meat helps rheumatoid arthritis. Eating less red and processed meat is good general health advice, and the NHS suggests cutting down to about 70g a day if you eat more than 90g. But you do not need to avoid it completely, and red meat is a good source of iron, which matters because anaemia is more common with inflammatory arthritis.

Myth 16: "You can never drink alcohol if you take methotrexate"

Verdict: outdated for many people, but check with your team. Arthritis UK says it used to be thought that people taking methotrexate needed to avoid alcohol, but recent research suggests it is safe for people taking this drug to drink within the UK low-risk guideline of 14 units a week. Both alcohol and methotrexate can affect the liver, so drinking in moderation matters, and your rheumatology team may give you individual advice based on your blood tests. Alcohol also increases the risk of stomach problems and bleeding with NSAIDs, and drowsiness with some painkillers.

What is true

  • A balanced, Mediterranean-style diet supports overall health and is suggested by NICE for rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Oily fish has the strongest food evidence, mainly for rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Reaching a healthy weight helps osteoarthritis and general health.
  • Calcium and vitamin D matter for bone health.
  • For gout, diet genuinely matters: some foods high in purines and alcohol can trigger attacks.
  • Some foods and supplements interact with arthritis medicines, such as grapefruit with some drugs and vitamin K-rich foods with warfarin.

Why do diet myths spread?

Arthritis symptoms naturally go up and down. If you cut out a food just before a good spell, it is easy to conclude that the food was the problem. Testimonials are powerful, and the people selling diet books, tests and supplements benefit from bold claims. Arthritis UK suggests reading beyond the headline, checking whether claims are backed by research, using a fact-checking service such as Full Fact, and asking your healthcare team.

Myths are not always harmless. Cutting out several food groups at once can lead to low calcium, iron, fibre or protein, unplanned weight loss and a lot of stress around eating. Money spent on unproven tests, supplements and "special" products is money not spent on foods with real benefits. Most importantly, anyone who delays or stops proven treatment because of a diet claim risks their arthritis getting worse.

If you still think a food affects you

Your experience matters. If you suspect a food, keep a food and symptom diary for a few weeks, then, with advice from a doctor or dietitian, cut out one food completely for a few weeks and reintroduce it to see whether symptoms return. Arthritis UK recommends speaking to a doctor or dietitian first so the change is made safely and you do not miss out on nutrients.

When to see a dietitian

Ask your GP or rheumatology team about a referral to a registered dietitian if you are considering cutting out a food group, think you have a food intolerance, follow a restrictive diet, or are confused by conflicting advice. "Dietitian" is a protected title in the UK; dietitians must be registered with the HCPC.

When to get medical help

Do not stop prescribed arthritis medicines because of diet advice. Check with a pharmacist before taking supplements, especially if you take warfarin or other anticoagulants, methotrexate or NSAIDs. See your GP if you have gut symptoms, unexplained weight loss or think you have a food allergy. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever.

Frequently asked questions

Should I stop eating tomatoes if I have arthritis?

No, not unless you have a specific allergy. Arthritis UK says research has shown no link between nightshade vegetables and inflammation.

Is dairy bad for arthritis?

The evidence is mixed, and dairy is an important source of calcium. If you avoid it, choose calcium-fortified alternatives.

Does apple cider vinegar help joint pain?

Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that it improves arthritis symptoms.

Should I go gluten-free for arthritis?

Not unless you have coeliac disease or a diagnosed sensitivity. Get tested for coeliac disease before cutting out gluten if you have symptoms.

Can any diet cure arthritis?

No. No diet or supplement cures arthritis, but a healthy diet and weight support your overall health and can help some symptoms.

Why do some people say diet changes helped them?

Some people genuinely feel better, perhaps because of weight loss, a food intolerance or a healthier overall diet. Arthritis also naturally varies, which can make changes look more effective than they are.
